title: Conduct Continuous Cleaning and Sanitising of the Abattoir

lessons.title: Cleaning while the line is running
lessons.html:
What continuous cleaning means

In a pork abattoir, dirt builds up all day: blood, hair, scurf, fat, dung and bits of meat. If it stays on the floor, tables and equipment, germs grow and spread to the carcasses. Continuous cleaning means you clean during the shift, not only at the end of the day.

What you clean during the shift

  • Floors: push hair, fat and pieces of meat to the drains or pick them up into the correct bin. Keep walkways clear so nobody slips.
  • Hand-wash basins and knife sterilizers: check that they have water, soap and paper towels, and that sterilizers are hot.
  • Work stands, tables and trays: rinse off blood and fat often.
  • Bins: empty them before they overflow. Keep condemned and inedible bins closed and marked.
  • Drains: clear the drain covers so water can flow.

Rules while cleaning during production

  1. Never spray water near carcasses. Splash from the floor carries germs onto the meat.
  2. Use low pressure water during production, not a high-pressure jet.
  3. Do not use cleaning chemicals near meat unless the plant procedure allows it.
  4. Use the correct cleaning tools for each area. Many plants colour-code brushes and squeegees: for example, one colour for floors and another for food-contact surfaces. Never use a floor brush on a table.
  5. Tell the line workers before you clean near them.

Continuous cleaning keeps the abattoir safe, keeps the meat inspector satisfied, and makes the big clean at the end of the day easier.

lessons.title: The end-of-shift clean: step by step
lessons.html:
Cleaning and sanitising are different

Cleaning removes visible dirt, fat and blood. Sanitising kills most of the germs that are left. You cannot sanitise a dirty surface: dirt protects germs from the sanitiser. So you always clean first.

Steps for the end-of-shift clean

  1. Prepare. Make sure all meat has left the area. Switch off and lock out machines, following the lockout procedure. Cover electrical boxes if the procedure says so.
  2. Dry clean. Pick up or scrape off hair, fat, meat scraps and other solid waste. Put them in the correct bins.
  3. Pre-rinse. Rinse with warm water from top to bottom: ceilings and high equipment first, then walls, equipment, and floors last.
  4. Apply detergent. Use the detergent your plant gives you, mixed exactly as the label and procedure say. Foam or spray it on and let it work for the contact time stated.
  5. Scrub. Use brushes and pads to remove fat and stubborn dirt, especially in corners, under tables and on the de-hairer and conveyors.
  6. Rinse. Rinse off all detergent with clean water, top to bottom.
  7. Inspect. Look and feel. Surfaces must be free of fat, blood, hair and film. Clean again if not.
  8. Sanitise. Apply the sanitiser at the correct strength. Some sanitisers must be rinsed off and some are left on; follow the label.
  9. Dry and record. Squeegee water to the drains, store equipment, and sign the cleaning checklist.

lessons.title: Using cleaning chemicals safely
lessons.html:
Chemicals can hurt you

Abattoir detergents are often strong alkalis to remove fat, and some cleaners are acids to remove scale. Sanitisers may contain chlorine or other strong chemicals. They can burn skin and eyes and harm your lungs.

Always

  • Read the label and the safety data sheet (SDS), or ask your supervisor to explain them.
  • Wear the protective equipment the label and plant procedure require: rubber gloves, goggles or face shield, apron and boots.
  • Measure chemicals with the correct measuring jug or use the automatic dosing system.
  • Add chemical to water, not water to chemical.
  • Keep chemicals in their original, labelled containers.
  • Store chemicals in the locked chemical store, away from meat and packaging.

Never

  • Never mix different chemicals. For example, chlorine products mixed with acids give off a dangerous gas.
  • Never put chemicals in cool-drink bottles or food containers.
  • Never use more chemical than the label says. Stronger is not better; it is dangerous and leaves residues on surfaces.
  • Never point a hose or spray at another person.

If there is an accident

  • Chemical in the eye: rinse with lots of clean running water at the eye-wash station for a long time and call for help.
  • Chemical on skin: remove wet clothing and rinse the skin with plenty of water.
  • Report every accident to your supervisor. Take the label or SDS to the clinic.

First aid must be learned in hands-on training by an accredited provider.

Key points

  • Clean continuously during the shift, but never spray near carcasses.
  • Clean first, then sanitise.
  • Work from top to bottom and rinse off all detergent.
  • Mix chemicals exactly as the label says and never mix two chemicals together.
  • Wear gloves and eye protection, and sign the cleaning record.

quiz.question: What is the difference between cleaning and sanitising?

options.text: They are the same thing
Cleaning removes visible dirt; sanitising kills most remaining germs
Sanitising removes fat; cleaning kills germs
Sanitising is only done once a month

quiz.question: In which order do you rinse during the end-of-shift clean?

options.text: Floors first, then walls, then ceiling
Only the floors

Any order

options.text: Splash from the floor carries germs onto the meat

quiz.question: How should you mix a cleaning chemical?

Mix it in an empty cool-drink bottle
